Alienate

/AY-lee-uh-nayt/ - the stress falls on AY · verb

Hear It

What It Means

Alienate means to cause someone to feel unwelcome or estranged; to lose the support of.

By mocking the interns' questions in every meeting, the new director managed to alienate the very staff he needed most.

Worked Example

The homeowners' association banned street hockey, then towed a resident's van over a two-inch violation; within a year it had alienated so many neighbors that nobody would run for its board.

Alienate is more precise than 'annoy' or 'upset' because it names the lasting result, not the momentary sting—people who feel alienated stop feeling welcome and quietly withdraw their support, often for good.

How Alienate Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

estrange

estrange: suggests a deeper, often lasting breach, especially inside families

disaffect

disaffect: used of groups losing their loyalty to leaders or institutions

Antonyms

endear

endear: wins affection and closeness instead of losing it

charm

charm: actively draws people in

How Strong Is It? — offend → alienate → estrange

offend vs. alienate

offend vs. alienate: Offend is the milder word—an offended guest may grumble through dinner and still come back next week, while alienating someone drives them away.

estrange vs. alienate

estrange vs. alienate: Estrange goes further than offend or alienate—estranged relatives may not exchange a word for decades, the breach hardened into settled distance.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — alien

Root — alien: belonging to another (Latin alienus, from alius, 'other')

Suffix — -ate

Suffix — -ate: to make, to cause to be

Put it together

Put it together: Alien (belonging to another, from Latin alius, 'other') + -ate (to make) = to make someone feel like an outsider. Latin alienare meant 'to make a thing another's—to hand it away,' and English kept both senses: property can be alienated (signed away), and so can people's loyalty.

Use the root in a new word: inalienable

Use the root in a new word: inalienable: The declaration calls liberty an inalienable right—one that cannot be handed away or taken, because it belongs to you alone.

Word Choice

neutral / analytic

Alienate is the word for losing people—supporters, friends, allies—through your own actions. For a one-time insult, 'offend' is enough; reach for alienate when the damage sends people away for good. Note the direction of traffic in this unit: alienate pushes people away, while placate works to win angry ones back.
